 TOI Tech Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 17, 2026, 13:40 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium

 Print Nvidia’s ‘royal family’ and its harsh meetings Jensen Huang built a reputation as Silicon Valley's most charismatic boss, the showman in the leather jacket that employees queued up to take selfies with. A different picture of how he ran Nvidia is now coming out. The ousted CEO routinely told staff their questions and ideas were "stupid" in meetings, according to a Wall Street Journal report. His daughter Madison Huang, who effectively worked as his chief of staff, called employees who couldn't remember things "goldfish". The report, based on accounts from employees, describes a $5 trillion company that still ran like a family business. Huang, 63, had around 60 direct reports, and his two adult children and son-in-law all worked at the company. The report comes days after Huang resigned on November 12. His exit followed revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a customer executive whom US officials suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. China has denied the claim. Watch NEW: Trump's Big U-Turn On Nvidia Scandal? POTUS Declares Jensen Huang's Lover ‘Not A China Spy’ Not everyone sees the bluntness as a flaw. Rob Csongor, a former senior executive who retired in 2020, told the WSJ it was part of the formula. "One of the reasons why I believe Nvidia was successful was this intellectual honesty," he said. Jensen Huang's 'dead-face' remarks and the scoldings inside Nvidia 
 Others remember it differently. Several employees described a boss who dressed people down for weak ideas or a lack of urgency. After scolding people, he would sometimes call the blank looks around the table "dead-face". One executive called these sessions eviscerations, and they had reportedly become more frequent. In one recent meeting, Huang tore into senior executive Vladimir Troy in front of the group over delays to Nvidia's data-centre builds. The same CEO hosted summer parties for interns at his home and dropped by Shannon's, a bar inside Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters. Madison Huang, Nvidia's de facto chief of staff, faced staff complaints 
 Madison Huang, 35, trained as a chef and sommelier and worked at LVMH before joining Nvidia as a summer intern in 2020. She rose fast, sitting in on her father's quarterly executive meetings and presenting to the board, The New York Times reported. The NYT report includes an incident with a New Delhi link. Huang was due to headline a conference in the Indian capital in February but pulled out and sent longtime lieutenant Jay Puri instead. Ahead of the event, Madison berated employees on a call, Puri included. He eventually told her he would answer her questions once she stopped yelling. He left his role less than six months later. So many employees complained that HR made her attend weekly coaching sessions on her management style, per the NYT. Employees estimate that more than a dozen key executives left because they disliked working with her. "Nepotism is almost always a bad idea," Harvard Business School professor David Yoffie told the paper. Nvidia board not considering Jensen Huang's return despite Trump and Silicon Valley push 
 That leaves a hard call for interim CEO Colette Kress. She has clashed with Madison Huang over robotics investments and must now decide what role the Huang family keeps at the company. Outside Nvidia, much of Silicon Valley has lined up behind Huang. A "Stand with Jensen" letter seeking his reinstatement has crossed 180,000 signatures. Signatories include Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The letter says no evidence has been shown that the woman at the centre of the scandal was a spy. "Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen's leadership," it reads. Some have gone further. Venture capitalist David Sacks, a former White House AI and crypto adviser, has questioned the spy allegations, pointing to reports that US officials still cannot confirm them. Sweeney suggested the board had been pushed into its decision. Replit CEO Amjad Masad called the timing suspicious, given Huang's support for open AI models. Chip research firm SemiAnalysis floated a theory that Huang's exit clears the way for the Remote Access Security Act. Huang opposed the bill, which would extend export controls to cloud access to AI chips. Join conversation

 President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to Huang returning. The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Huang had discussed a comeback with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, however, told CNBC that Huang had not raised it with him. The board is not considering it, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. Directors are focused on an investigation by law firm Wachtell Lipton into whether Huang's conduct compromised national security or company secrets. They are also choosing a search firm to find the next CEO.
